title: 'Godzilla El Niño' is wreaking havoc with Philippine central bank's inflation forecasts
description: Eli Remolona, governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Spring meetings at the IMF head
body: Eli Remolona, governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Spring meetings at the IMF headquarters in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, April 25, 2025.  Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK — The Philippine central bank is planning for a "Godzilla" El Niño on top of a prolonged oil shock, as the Southeast Asian nation tries to rein in inflation from three-year highs.Governor Eli Remolona said Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas now sets policy using scenarios that factor in oil prices and the severity of the weather event. "We have the regular, ordinary El Niño, which is bad, and then we have the Godzilla El Niño, which is really, really bad," he said Wednesday on a panel at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.The worst of El Niño's impact on prices is still to come, with the effects expected from November through February, he said, adding that maintaining price stability remains the central bank's priority.  "We're holding our breath," he said, "but we have to be prepared for the worst."The looming weather risk is adding fresh pressure on one of Southeast Asia's most vulnerable economies. Philippine inflation accelerated to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, with rice prices up 18%, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority. The world's biggest rice importer is also exposed to food supply risk. Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel has warned that a fresh drought could squeeze domestic supply. Larger Philippine purchases could add demand to a global market already jolted by El Niño and export curbs. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization has raised its rice price index for six consecutive months to a 20-month high.   The central bank lifted its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 5% in August to keep a lid on the runaway inflation. The BSP should deliver another quarter-percentage hike next week to 5.25%, followed by another same-sized hike in December, according to Aris Dacanay, senior ASEAN economist at HSBC Bank, in a note Wednesday.

schema.headline: 'Godzilla El Niño' is wreaking havoc with Philippine central bank's inflation forecasts

title: South Korean carmaker Hyundai plans 'strategic' investment of $15.5 billion in India by 2032
description: MUMBAI, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA - 2024/10/21: Hyundai logo is seen on the Hyundai car showroom in Mumbai. Hyundai Initial Public Offer (IPO) will be listed
body: MUMBAI, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA - 2024/10/21: Hyundai logo is seen on the Hyundai car showroom in Mumbai. Hyundai Initial Public Offer (IPO) will be listed on the stock exchange on 22nd October 2024. (Photo by Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's Hyundai Motor Group on Tuesday said it plans to invest $15.5 billion from 2026 through 2032 in India, a market it considers core to the company's emerging-market growth and expansion."India remains one of Hyundai Motor Group's most important and strategic markets globally," Euisun Chung, the executive chair of Hyundai Motor Group, said in a release following his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.He added that this investment "reaffirms" the company's commitment to the Indian market for the next 30 years and beyond. Over the seven-year plan, Hyundai said it will invest across manufacturing expansion and in developing research and development infrastructure, local supplier cultivation for parts localization, and future technology innovation.To execute these investments, Hyundai will set up a dedicated investment entity in India, it said in the release.The Indian car market has been hitting new records every month, driven by strong demand. In August, passenger car sales hit a new monthly record with sales of 439,000 units, over 36% higher year-on-year, as per data from industry body Society of Indian Auto Manufacturers. Hyundai is the third-largest car company in India and sold 247,980 passenger cars in the country between April and August this year, according to data released last month.Japanese carmaker Maruti Suzuki was the top seller in the country over that period, followed by India's Mahindra & Mahindra, as per SIAM's data. However, in the financial year ended March 2026, Hyundai came in fourth, edged out by M&M and Tata Motors. Hyundai has a total production capacity of 1.4 million vehicles across India and exports cars from these locations. In 2024, the South Korean company listed its India business unit, Hyundai Motors India, raising $3.3 billion in the largest-ever initial public offer in the country.

schema.headline: South Korean carmaker Hyundai plans 'strategic' investment of $15.5 billion in India by 2032

title: China's exports and imports surge past expectations in September
description: Chinese-made cars are seen in specialised vehicle racks in preparation for loading onto ships for export, at the Taicang Port area of Suzhou Port, in
body: Chinese-made cars are seen in specialised vehicle racks in preparation for loading onto ships for export, at the Taicang Port area of Suzhou Port, in China's eastern Jiangsu province on October 12, 2026. - | Afp | Getty ImagesBEIJING — China's exports grew by 36.3% in September from a year ago, their fastest pace since February, according to official data released Wednesday.Imports climbed by 31%, the fastest increase since June, the data showed, picking up from 28.2% in August.Both exports and imports exceeded estimates from a Reuters poll, of 25.5% and 24.5%, respectively. China's exports to the U.S. grew by nearly 39.6% in September, outpacing the growth of overall exports and sending the monthly trade surplus to the highest since January 2025, according to customs data accessed via Wind Information.The value of China's integrated circuit board exports globally surged by 136% in September from a year ago — but the number of units exported only rose by 1%, according to CNBC calculations of official figures. The volume of China's crude oil imports fell by double-digits for a sixth-straight month, even as their value rose for the first time since May, according to Wind. China's crude oil and natural gas imports have both declined in volume since the start of the year.Earlier this year, China's exports and imports each grew at their fastest pace in five years.A surge in demand for China-made parts for data centers to power artificial intelligence has helped fuel exports, along with stabilization in tensions with the U.S., China's largest trading partner on a single-country basis."The resulting trade surplus of $133.5 billion, a record monthly high, underscores the continued strength of China's external sector despite lingering concerns over domestic demand," Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International Holdings, said in a note.Global scrutiny on the economic impact of China's surging exports has escalated in recent years, amid sluggish domestic demand. AI-related demand and a coinciding rise in prices of core products have also helped support import growth.The U.S. and China last month announced plans to roll back tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, and extend a broader trade truce by two months to January.The European Union last week announced China agreed to halve its exports of hybrid-powered cars to the bloc, following high-level trade talks in Beijing.China's overall car exports surged by 56.3% in September to 1.18 million vehicles, with the value of those exports climbing by 62%, the data showed. For the first three quarters of the year, China's exports grew to every major country tracked by the customs agency. However, imports from Malaysia, Germany and the U.K. fell during that time.Reflecting the impact of export controls and stockpiling, the volume of China's rare earths and fertilizer exports dropped during the first three-quarters of this year, while fertilizer imports surged.

schema.headline: China's exports and imports surge past expectations in September

title: China's producer prices rise at fastest pace since June 2022, beating expectations
description: Citizens are shopping at a supermarket in Nanjing, East China's Jiangsu province, on March 9, 2024. Costfoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChina's producer
body: Citizens are shopping at a supermarket in Nanjing, East China's Jiangsu province, on March 9, 2024. Costfoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChina's producer price index climbed at its fastest pace in over four years, rising 5% in September as higher fuel prices pushed up costs for businesses. The increase was higher than the 4.5% expected by economists polled by Reuters, and sharply up from  the 3.8% seen in the previous month. China's National Bureau of Statistics said higher prices were also seen in the country's coal sector, due to increased demand for coal for winter heating, temporary tight supply in major coal-producing areas, and expectations of rising international coal prices.Consumer prices saw a 0.9% rise, marginally missing expectations of 1%, but up from 0.8% in the month before.The increase in the consumer inflation rate was due to gasoline prices, which climbed 16.6% and contributed approximately 0.47 percentage points to the year-on-year CPI increase, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the Urban Division at the NBS.This was partially offset by a wider fall in food prices, which declined 1.7% and pulled down the CPI by 0.29 percentage points, Dong added.The core CPI rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed 1%.The lower-than-expected CPI reading indicates that domestic demand remains "lackluster," according to Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, in a note after the data release.However, the higher PPI is pointing to an economy that is gradually moving away from deflationary pressures even if the recovery remains uneven, said Hao Zhou, chief economist at Guotai Junan International Holdings.His view was that domestic demand was recovering more gradually than the industrial sector, although the fact that consumer inflation has remained in positive territory indicated at the deflationary environment in 2024 and 2025 "is continuing to fade."The higher inflation figures come as China's economy grapples with its lowest growth rate in more than three years. GDP growth for the second quarter of the year missed expectations at 4.3%. While economic data for August showed that retail sales expanded more slowly than expected, industrial output beat expectations.On Sept 28, a State Council readout signaled that more policy support could be on the way for the Chinese economy, saying that "In response to emerging challenges in the economy's operation, efforts should be made to intensify counter-cyclical adjustment of macro policies."Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, wrote that "It marks a bit of a shift in tone," adding that more policy support rollouts will be coming so as to reach both short- and long-term growth targets."These include the 4.5%-5.0% GDP growth target for 2026, and the longstanding goal to double GDP from 2020 to 2035."

schema.headline: China's producer prices rise at fastest pace since June 2022, beating expectations

title: Crypto bosses, CEOs and F1: Singapore's business events boom gathers pace
description: SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 11: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains and Charles
body: SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 11: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains and Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 battle for the race lead at the start during the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 11, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Joe Portlock/Getty Images)Joe Portlock | Getty Images Sport | Getty ImagesBillionaires, global CEOs and crypto executives descended on Singapore last week as a growing number of high-profile conferences coincided with the country's Formula 1 Grand Prix.More than 40 business events were held around this year's Grand Prix period, up from over 25 in 2025 and over 30 in 2024, according to the Singapore Tourism Board. The events included the Milken Institute Asia Summit, TOKEN2049, the Forbes Global CEO Conference, Solana Summit APAC and the Global-Asia Family Office Summit.Formula 1 has generated more than 2.2 billion Singapore dollars ($1.72 billion) in incremental tourism receipts between its debut in 2008 and 2024, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, which equates to an average of S$150 million each. The race itself costs approximately S$140 million a year to organize, METI said, though noted it isn't directly comparable with the revenue generated.Singapore GP said the 2026 race drew 301,294 spectators, the second-highest attendance in the event's history.Business events themselves are becoming a larger source of tourism revenue. Receipts from meetings, incentives, conventions and exhibitions (MICE) rose 35% to S$2.3 billion in 2025, outpacing the 10% growth in Singapore's overall tourism receipts to a record S$32.8 billion, data from STB showed.Singapore's Tourism Board noted that MICE visitors typically spend significantly more than leisure travelers.Organizers are increasingly capitalizing on the excitement surrounding Formula 1 to extend delegates' stays, according to Poh Chi Chuan, executive director of exhibitions and conferences at STB."This creates a natural gravitational pull, when the city is buzzing and the right target audience is already flying in, savvy planners build on that momentum," Poh said.At TOKEN2049, one of the world's major cryptocurrency conferences, overseas attendees accounted for 85.6% of participants this year, up from 82.7% in 2025, according to figures provided by the event organizer. The figures classify overseas attendees as those who are not Singaporean nationals.Chinese attendees accounted for 11.8% of participants, nearly double the 6% share recorded last year, overtaking Americans as the largest group.The influx of business travelers also coincided with strong demand at Singapore's luxury hotels.Marina Bay Sands said its hotel, the iconic three-towered building often featured in photos of the Singapore skyline, operated at near-full occupancy during the Formula 1 period.The integrated resort also hosted TOKEN2049 at its Expo & Convention Centre, underscoring how major business conferences and sporting events are increasingly overlapping.For the hotel industry overall, the clustering of MICE events and Formula 1 helped propel rates to record levels last year.In October 2025, average room rates rose 19.5% from a year earlier to S$384.15, according to hospitality data provider CoStar. On the opening day of that race weekend, hotel occupancy reached 95.9% and the average room rate jumped to S$757.62.

schema.headline: Crypto bosses, CEOs and F1: Singapore's business events boom gathers pace

title: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure
description: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian m
body: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations. It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions. Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday."There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday.He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday."The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel. Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement. Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Starlink disruptionsZelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the StarShield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.SpaceX and the White House have been contacted for comment.

schema.headline: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure

title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts
description: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to acces
body: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call."You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers.  The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access.A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers."Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said."We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added.That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful.There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added.'Liability transfer'Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely.In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents.Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer."Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example.Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month.  In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts.

schema.headline: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts

title: Judge extends block on Trump White House ban of MS NOW, CNN and Politico
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to the press before boarding Marine One as he departs from the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, on Oc
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to the press before boarding Marine One as he departs from the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, on Oct. 12, 2026. Brendan Smialowski | AFP | Getty ImagesA federal judge late Tuesday night indefinitely extended his block on the White House from enforcing a ban on three media outlets that President Donald Trump announced in mid-September.The preliminary injunction by Judge Timothy Kelly replaces his temporary restraining order against Trump's ban of MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House complex as a lawsuit challenging the ban plays out."President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him," wrote Kelly, who was nominated by Trump for his seat in U.S. District Court in Washington.In his written opinion, Kelly said the three outlets were likely to succeed on their claim in their pending lawsuit, which argues they were denied due process when Trump summarily barred them without giving them a chance to argue against it.The judge cited two existing opinions by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which establish a due process right to journalists whose White House passes are targeted for revocation. Those appellate opinions are binding on federal District Court judges in D.C.The judge also said, for the first time in this case, the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which allege retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.Kelly's order Tuesday is not a final ruling on the merits of the suit. And it does not compel the White House to restore access to the Oval Office and Air Force One to the outlets.Kelly brushed aside the Department of Justice's claim that in addition to concerns about inaccurate news stories, Trump decided to revoke the outlets' access to the White House on national security grounds."There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote.The judge said the DOJ's national security argument appears to be "merely a post-hoc justification for the decision" after the outlets sued."Still, no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed," Kelly wrote."That said, for the reasons explained below, the Court will extend the relief it already ordered, which will continue to preserve the status quo while this case proceeds," Kelly said, referring to his prior order that restored access by the outlets to the White House.The judge said that without the preliminary injunction, the outlets were "likely to suffer irreparable harm."His ruling came on the heels of a court hearing last Thursday, when the DOJ defended the ban, which reportedly led to 78 journalists having their so-called hard passes to the White House revoked before Kelly ordered them restored with his previous temporary restraining order.Trump last month said he would appeal any decision by Kelly blocking his ban. CNBC has requested comment from the White House and DOJ.Theodore Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, said in a statement, "We are grateful that the Court ruled in favor of our clients.""When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said. "Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.""The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," the attorney said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this "unconstitutional ban on the free press" for the foreseeable future."Trump on Sept. 18 said that he was banning the three outlets because of how they have covered him.In a Truth Social post that day, Trump wrote that the outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."Trump later said that same day that he had become "sick" of "cumulative stories" by the outlets.The ban took effect on the following day, Sept. 19, when journalists from the outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their permanent passes confiscated by Secret Service officers.The outlets sued Trump on Sept. 21 in a civil complaint that said, "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles." Kelly, two days later, issued a restraining order that temporarily reversed the ban for at least 14 days. Journalists from the three outlets on Sept. 24 were allowed to return to the White House, and since then Kelly extended the restraining order to allow him time to consider whether to issue Tuesday's preliminary injunction, which has no set expiration date.

schema.headline: Judge extends block on Trump White House ban of MS NOW, CNN and Politico

title: Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says
description: WASILLA, ALASKA - OCTOBER 13: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an election rally at the Menard Memorial Sports Center on October 13, 2026 in
body: WASILLA, ALASKA - OCTOBER 13: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an election rally at the Menard Memorial Sports Center on October 13, 2026 in Wasilla, Alaska. President Trump is in Alaska campaigning for local Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Alex Wong | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska."Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years," Trump said at a rally in Alaska. "That guarantees a success."His latest remarks follow repeated claims earlier this month that South Korea had agreed to join the $50 billion Alaska LNG project, even as Seoul maintained that its participation had not been finalized. "We'll also invest $4.4 billion into the project, on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea to Alaska," Trump said.However, the terms of the Taiwan deal cited by Trump were not immediately clear.Last year, Taiwan's state-owned energy company CPC Corp reportedly reached an agreement with Alaska Gasline Development Corp to purchase LNG and invest in the pipeline project.Taiwan, home to critical semiconductor giant TSMC, has seen energy demand climb due to AI-related growth. However, the island relies on imports for more than 90% of its energy supply and this summer projected its average electricity demand growth rate through 2035 would exceed that of Japan and South Korea.Taiwan's economic affairs ministry said that growth rate would climb by about 2.5% a year, the second-highest forecast in its history. The democratically self-ruled island is still waiting on major new arms sales from the U.S. Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory.Glenfarne, the developer of the Alaska LNG pipeline, told the U.S. government in a report this month the project aims to deliver its first gas in 2029.Trump has also stepped up pressure on South Korea over its participation in the project, warning earlier this month that he would charge the country more and threatened to double the charges if Seoul failed to sign soon, without specifying what would be doubled. That prompted speculation in South Korean media that he was referring to higher tariffs.The White House, Taiwan's energy ministry and CPC Corp. did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

schema.headline: Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says

title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
description: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters i
body: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, April 30, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAnthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models."The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation."The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models.Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety."In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation. Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation.— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report. WATCH: Anthropic poised to disclose new revenue numbers watch now

schema.headline: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting

title: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name
description: Elon Musk, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (L) and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick (C), speaks during a press event with US Preside
body: Elon Musk, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (L) and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick (C), speaks during a press event with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on May 30, 2025. Allison Robbert | AFP | Getty ImagesA federal magistrate judge in Virginia ruled that Elon Musk engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans when he posted falsehoods on X last year accusing her of "criminal action" and of "funneling $58 million to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan." Musk, the world's richest person, was working for the Trump administration as the head of DOGE when he shared those posts on Feb. 11, 2025. The Department of Homeland Security said the next day it was firing Comans and three colleagues, and labeled them "deep state activists." In Tuesday's order, U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cleared Comans' name.Comans served as FEMA CFO from around January 2018 until February 2025, and was also FEMA's operating chief from 2020 to 2021. Fitzpatrick wrote in the order that, "The facts establish that high-ranking government officials," including Musk, then a special government employee, had "engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans.""Mr. Musk was the head of DOGE, he knew or should have known that any payments made to state or local governments through a FEMA grant in February 2025 were approved by his subordinates," the judge wrote. He added that Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans "to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action,'" an act Fitzpatrick described as "little more than state sanctioned intimidation."CNBC has reached out to Musk and White House attorneys involved in the case for comment.Democracy Defenders Fund, which was involved in Comans' case, said in a statement that it was pleased with the decision. "Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years," said Craig Becker, the group's head of affirmative litigation. "Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain."WATCH: Musk says jobs are going to change because of AIwatch now

schema.headline: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name

title: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
description: A man holds a smartphone beside an electronic display showing the Hang Seng Index beneath Hang Seng Bank's logo and signage on October 12, 2026 in Hon
body: A man holds a smartphone beside an electronic display showing the Hang Seng Index beneath Hang Seng Bank's logo and signage on October 12, 2026 in Hong Kong, China. Cheng Xin | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesBEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs.The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research, said on a podcast that the investment bank published Tuesday.Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, to accelerate plans for entering other countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans to enter Canada next year.Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners.Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors. Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance.Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years. That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said.But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%. The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors."Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. "Brands are becoming long-term, embedded competitors capable of reshaping market dynamics across Latin America.

schema.headline: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas

title: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says
description: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (L) speaks with US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent ahead of a morning work meeting to "revive balanced,
body: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (L) speaks with US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent ahead of a morning work meeting to "revive balanced, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth for the benefit of all" in the presence of the G7 countries, partner countries, the International Monetary Fund, and the OECD, as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026.  Ludovic Marin | Afp | Getty ImagesBANGKOK — The head of the International Monetary Fund has urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to trim the deficit, warning that his plan to lean on growth to tame U.S. Government debt isn't sufficient."Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel Wednesday at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "Some [fiscal] measures would be necessary."Georgieva said Bessent recognizes that federal deficits and overall debt have grown "too high," and that measures to improve the budget balance and reduce the debt are necessary. But "the authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to bring them down, she said.Bessent and Trump administration officials have touted resilient economic growth, driven by the artificial-intelligence build-out, reshoring manufacturing and tax cuts for consumers, as crucial tools to improve the U.S. fiscal posture."With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this," Bessent said last month. He has argued sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt ratio and bend the debt-to-GDP curve. U.S. federal debt has exceeded 100% of gross domestic product, once an unthinkable threshold, with the country's public debt load surpassing $40 trillion and on track to break a record set in the aftermath of World War II. The U.S. government has historically spent more than it collects through taxation, committing to unbalanced spending in the decades since President Bill Clinton briefly managed to balance the budget in the 1990s. But debt-financed spending has sharply accelerated in recent years. Trump cut taxes in his first term and signed the first Covid relief packages in 2020, which Joe Biden followed with a $1.9 trillion stimulus in 2021. watch nowThat federal spending helped stave off a recession but also fueled inflation that still weighs on American households and businesses. Before his appointment, Bessent had said he wanted Trump to cut the deficit to less than 4% of GDP by the end of his term, and said in August that the U.S. budget deficit had likely peaked. The U.S. Treasury market has been battered this year with yields climbing to multidecade highs, as investors bet that surging energy costs and heavy AI spending will keep borrowing costs higher. Benchmark 10-year yields hovered near their highest level since 2002, standing at around 5.2% on Wednesday.  Debt pile growsAlthough the budget figures for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 have not yet been released, the deficit is expected to top 6% of GDP, compared with 5.8% in fiscal 2025."With the government running an annual budget deficit of 6 percent of GDP, the debt will rise another $7 billion by the end of today—and each subsequent day," Benn Steil, senior fellow and director of international economics at Council on Foreign Relations, said in a Sept.25 note.  Steil also warned that it could be "reckless" for Washington to declare the debt crunch solved by supporting unsupported projections, pressing for spending and revenue reforms. The IMF, which released its October World Economic Outlook on Tuesday, forecasts U.S. growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and projects U.S. gross government debt reaching 142% of GDP by 2031. IMF chief Georgieva has also urged governments to set credible medium-term plans to control deficits instead of relying on stronger growth alone, as global public debt heads toward 100% of GDP before the end of the decade, the highest since World War II. Bessent reportedly missed this week's meetings to attend to "domestic engagements."

schema.headline: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says

title: Diesel squeeze set to last well into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA says
description: A garbage truck drives past gas prices above $6 a gallon and diesel prices above $8 a gallon as they are displayed outside of a Shell gas station in C
body: A garbage truck drives past gas prices above $6 a gallon and diesel prices above $8 a gallon as they are displayed outside of a Shell gas station in Carson, California on September 22, 2026. Patrick T. Fallon | Afp | Getty ImagesConstraints on the diesel market will extend well into next year, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday. In its October Oil Market Report, the IEA said supply would remain tight into the latter half of 2027. A counter-seasonal tightening in gasoil markets in the third quarter, combined with "much heavier-than-normal inventory declines" in the preceding three months, had "deprived global gasoil markets of crucial stock cover ahead of the peak winter demand season," the IEA said. Last month saw global diesel exports drop by 700,000 barrels a day year-on-year, according to IEA data. A 1.3 million barrels per day loss from Russia and the Middle East was "only partly offset by higher supply from other sources," the agency said. watch nowBut while higher prices had weakened oil demand more broadly, the IEA said "relatively price inelastic diesel demand has remained strong," supported by government measures aimed at easing high prices for consumers. "Falling inventories, soaring cracks, and steepening levels of backwardation have signalled the need for additional supplies," it said. "However, even with a rapid recovery expected in refinery throughputs into year-end, gasoil supply falls short of meeting demand in 4Q26, suggesting that the replenishment of lost inventories, outside of typical seasonal fluctuations, is unlikely before [the second half of 2027]."The IEA pointed out that wholesale diesel prices exceeded $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and reached all-time highs of around $220 per barrel in Europe and the United States. "Retail diesel prices have risen in tandem to record levels in most major economies," it said in its report. But it warned that tensions in the crude freight market meant delivered diesel prices in the dominant gasoil importing markets – Europe, Africa and Latin America – could rise again in the coming weeks.Trump strikes Russian diesel deal to ease consumer squeeze U.S. diesel prices hit $6 a gallon for the first time last month, as the Iran war continued to impact global energy markets, with some market watchers warning elevated prices could linger for months to come. Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had made a deal with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin for Russia to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the global market, in a bid to offset sharp price rises sparked by Iran war-driven supply constraints. Read moreRussian energy has been harshly sanctioned by Western governments since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Trump's deal with Putin faced bipartisan condemnation in the U.S., with lawmakers in Europe also criticizing the move. Speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday, Valdis Dombrovskis, European Commissioner for the Economy and Productivity, warned "now is not a time to ease sanctions on Russia.""If we discuss this diesel deal specifically, it's worth noting that the volumes which are being discussed are anyway not going to have any macroeconomic significance, and the big question mark if Russia is able to deliver them anyway," he said. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday warned the deal contradicts efforts to get Putin to the negotiating table with Ukraine. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent crude continues to top $100 a barrel amid conflict-related supply disruption Oil demand destruction The IEA forecast that overall oil demand would fall by an average of 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026. Diesel will register 25% of that demand drop, the agency said. Oil supply, meanwhile, was forecast to post an average annual decline of 5.8 million barrels per day this year, before reversing course to rise by 7.7 million barrels per day in 2027. However, the IEA warned that "renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile."Over the past week, the Saudi capital Riyadh has come under a series of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, with some of the strikes resulting in fatalities. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco had been targeted overnight. Attacks on Saudi Arabia risked derailing the market recovery, the IEA said in its report, with Saudi production increases in September driving OPEC+ supply gains that month.

schema.headline: Diesel squeeze set to last well into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA says

title: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
description: U.S. President Donald Trump stands with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base El
body: U.S. President Donald Trump stands with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. Kevin Lamarque | ReutersMore Republicans are speaking out against President Donald Trump's decision to let Vladimir Putin's Russia temporarily export diesel fuel on the global market, expanding the bipartisan blowback over the deal.Six GOP senators joined six of their Democratic colleagues in a letter Tuesday urging Trump to cancel the arrangement allowing Russia to supply 4.8 million metric tons, or nearly 36 million barrels, of diesel through mid-April."This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the lawmakers wrote.Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Kentucky's Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn of Texas signed on, adding to the list of of GOP Congress members who had earlier questioned the deal Trump announced Friday. Armstrong has roots in the energy industry, having been CEO of Williams Companies, the largest natural gas-focused company in the U.S.They joined Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, New Hampshire's Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Durbin of Illinois, Delaware's Chris Coons and Rhode Island's Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed.The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the letter.Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had already spoken out, joining a statement with Democrats on Sunday that urged Trump not to "provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians."Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah had also joined that statement.Trump announced the Russia diesel deal after a call with Putin. The announcement quickly drew an unusually critical response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who counts on continued U.S. support for his military. Trump, in turn, slammed Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should get a new president.Trump claimed in Friday's announcement that the deal will help quickly and sharply bring record-high diesel prices down. But oil analysts don't think the Russian supply will be nearly enough to make a meaningful impact on prices.The 12 senators who signed Tuesday's letter to Trump agreed, writing that the deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans.""Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans," the senators told Trump."It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea," they wrote.The senators also alleged, as other critics already have, that the diesel deal contradicts the bipartisan Russian sanctions law that Trump signed into law a few weeks before announcing the deal, which required lifting existing sanctions on Russia. "These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," their letter read."Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," they wrote. "Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world."Trump has doubled down on his decision. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" he wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

schema.headline: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
